title: Observer
summary: Publish events to dependents without hard-wiring their concrete classes.

parts.rule: Observer lets subscribers register for notifications from a subject. The subject publishes an event through a subscriber interface instead of naming concrete listeners. Define whether delivery is synchronous, whether order is meaningful, what happens when one listener fails, and how a listener unsubscribes.
parts.why: A model that directly calls every view, analytics hook, and plugin accumulates dependencies each time a reaction is added. Observer lets those reactions vary independently. It also makes control flow less visible: one innocent update may trigger many callbacks, retain dead objects, or fail halfway through a listener list.
parts.example: A Document begins at version 6 with text "hello world". Three panels subscribe to DocumentChanged: Preview renders HTML, WordCount displays 2, and SaveIndicator marks the file dirty. setText("hello brave world") commits version 7, then emits DocumentChanged(version=7). The subject copies its current subscriber list before iterating, so a panel that unsubscribes during its callback does not corrupt the loop. Preview renders the new text, WordCount becomes 3, and SaveIndicator turns on. The UI contract says listener order is unspecified and one listener exception is recorded while the remaining listeners still run. When the WordCount panel closes, it calls the unsubscribe function returned by subscribe(); otherwise the Document would keep the panel alive and leak memory. Autosave may also observe the event, but durable document storage should not rely on a best-effort callback if saving is required before success is shown. Make that operation explicit. Across services, publishing the same event to a durable broker introduces retries, duplicate delivery, and consumer lag; that is message-driven architecture, not merely an in-memory Observer diagram. State those delivery semantics instead of assuming the local callback rules still apply.
parts.use: Use observer for in-process UI updates, plugin hooks, model-view synchronization, and non-critical domain notifications when the subscriber set changes independently of the subject. Keep events specific, expose an unsubscribe path, and make callback execution policy visible in the API or documentation.
parts.refuse: Use a direct collaborator when exactly one required action must succeed before the operation completes. Avoid long synchronous observer chains on a latency-sensitive path. Do not depend on accidental registration order, and do not keep strong references to short-lived listeners forever. For cross-process delivery, choose and describe a queue or event-bus protocol explicitly.

body:
Rule. Observer lets subscribers register for notifications from a subject. The subject publishes an event through a subscriber interface instead of naming concrete listeners. Define whether delivery is synchronous, whether order is meaningful, what happens when one listener fails, and how a listener unsubscribes.

Why it matters. A model that directly calls every view, analytics hook, and plugin accumulates dependencies each time a reaction is added. Observer lets those reactions vary independently. It also makes control flow less visible: one innocent update may trigger many callbacks, retain dead objects, or fail halfway through a listener list.

Worked example. A Document begins at version 6 with text "hello world". Three panels subscribe to DocumentChanged: Preview renders HTML, WordCount displays 2, and SaveIndicator marks the file dirty. setText("hello brave world") commits version 7, then emits DocumentChanged(version=7). The subject copies its current subscriber list before iterating, so a panel that unsubscribes during its callback does not corrupt the loop. Preview renders the new text, WordCount becomes 3, and SaveIndicator turns on. The UI contract says listener order is unspecified and one listener exception is recorded while the remaining listeners still run. When the WordCount panel closes, it calls the unsubscribe function returned by subscribe(); otherwise the Document would keep the panel alive and leak memory. Autosave may also observe the event, but durable document storage should not rely on a best-effort callback if saving is required before success is shown. Make that operation explicit. Across services, publishing the same event to a durable broker introduces retries, duplicate delivery, and consumer lag; that is message-driven architecture, not merely an in-memory Observer diagram. State those delivery semantics instead of assuming the local callback rules still apply.

[[diagram:notify]]

[[diagram:observer-flow]]

When to use. Use observer for in-process UI updates, plugin hooks, model-view synchronization, and non-critical domain notifications when the subscriber set changes independently of the subject. Keep events specific, expose an unsubscribe path, and make callback execution policy visible in the API or documentation.

When to refuse. Use a direct collaborator when exactly one required action must succeed before the operation completes. Avoid long synchronous observer chains on a latency-sensitive path. Do not depend on accidental registration order, and do not keep strong references to short-lived listeners forever. For cross-process delivery, choose and describe a queue or event-bus protocol explicitly.
